title: What If You Couldn't Recognize Faces? About 1 in 33 People Can't

scenes.text: What if you couldn't recognise your best friend's face? One in 33 people can't. Most don't know.
It's called face blindness. In 2023, Harvard researchers tested 3,341 people. 3.08 percent met the criteria.
That's more than 10 million Americans. Older estimates said only 2 to 2.5 percent.
31 of the 3,341 had the severe form, about 1 in 108. 72 had a milder form, about 1 in 47.
There was no sharp line. Face recognition sits on a continuum, like height. Some people are simply at the bottom of it.
So you might pass someone you've met ten times and see a stranger. You'd learn voices and walks instead. Millions do.

description:
What if you couldn't recognise faces, even familiar ones? About 1 in 33 people have some degree of prosopagnosia, or face blindness, according to a 2023 Harvard Medical School and VA Boston study of 3,341 people published in Cortex.
3.08 percent met the criteria, more than 10 million Americans, against older estimates of 2 to 2.5 percent; 1 in 108 had the major form and 1 in 47 a milder one, and face recognition turned out to be a continuum with no sharp cut-off.
